title: He's 15, He Has His Own Dressing Room, and England Is Already Trying to Tire Him Out
excerpt: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi heads to England with safeguarding protocols, tactical mind games from Michael Vaughan, and an Ireland humiliation hanging over India's camp.
body:
India's most talked-about cricketer this summer isn't Virat Kohli, Jasprit Bumrah, or any of the senior stars preparing for the England tour. It's a 15-year-old from Bihar who will need a separate changing room at every venue he plays.

Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, the left-handed opener who rewrote the IPL record books with 776 runs at a strike rate of 237.30 and a jaw-dropping 72 sixes, arrives in England this week for a five-match T20I series starting Wednesday, July 1 in Durham. He carries the expectations of a billion fans. He also carries his parents, who will travel with him under special BCCI arrangement — staying at the team hotel, which itself required an exemption from the usual protocol.

And he will not be sharing a dressing room with his teammates.

## The Safeguarding Protocols

Under ICC and ECB regulations for players under 16, Sooryavanshi must use a designated separate changing area at each of the five venues on the England tour. He can access the Indian dressing room during matches and attend team meetings. But before and after play, the teenager is on his own.

The ECB confirmed that county safeguarding officers at each venue are working with the team liaison officer to ensure the protocols are followed. "Each county safeguarding officer for the relevant cricket venue is also working closely with the team liaison officer to ensure venue protocols and arrangements are understood and adhered to," the board said.

It is an unprecedented situation in modern cricket — a player good enough to be the most feared batsman on either side, yet too young to share a changing room with his own team.

## Vaughan's Game Plan

Former England captain Michael Vaughan isn't worried about the protocols. He's worried about the cricket. And he thinks he's found Sooryavanshi's weakness.

"The one thing he's going to have to cope with is his fielding," Vaughan said on Ajinkya Rahane's YouTube channel. "There's no impact sub where he can sit on the bench. If I were England, I'd ask India to field first because then by the time Sooryavanshi comes to bat, he might be tired."

In the IPL, Sooryavanshi was often used as an impact substitute for Rajasthan Royals, meaning he could walk in fresh to bat without fielding for 20 overs. International cricket offers no such luxury. As an opener, if England bat first, Sooryavanshi will need to field through the entire innings before walking out to face a pumped-up English attack with a Dukes ball on a seaming English deck.

Vaughan went further, arguing that Sooryavanshi has single-handedly pushed T20 par scores to 230-plus — a testament to his impact, and a warning that England must find ways to neutralise him.

## The Ireland Shadow

The timing of this discussion couldn't be worse for India. Shreyas Iyer's side was swept 2-0 by Ireland in Belfast — India's first bilateral T20I series loss in more than two years. Jai Moondra, the Rajasthan-born fast bowler playing for Ireland, was named player of the series after taking 3-32 in the second match and dismissing the Indian top three in the first three overs.

And through both defeats, Sooryavanshi sat on the bench. Despite calls from fans, pundits, and former cricketers to unleash the teenager, India's team management chose to keep him out of the playing XI in both matches.

The question that now hangs over Indian cricket: would the outcome have been different if Sooryavanshi had played? India's senior batters — Sanju Samson, Abhishek Sharma, and Iyer himself — all fell cheaply. Tilak Varma's fighting 55 in the second match kept India within one run of victory, but it wasn't enough.

## What Awaits in England

The five-match T20I series against England is a different beast entirely. The series begins in Durham on July 1, with matches to follow across five iconic English cricket grounds. The English summer conditions — overcast skies, swing, variable bounce — will test every Indian batsman.

For NRIs across the UK, this is the cricket event of the summer. Indian fans in London, Birmingham, Manchester, and beyond have been tracking Sooryavanshi's trajectory since the IPL. Many saw Sangakkara's viral quote about the teenager's bat speed sounding "like a gunshot." They've watched the highlight reels. Now they might get to see him live, in person, on English soil.

After the England T20Is, India will stay for three ODIs starting July 14, with Shubman Gill as captain and Kohli returning subject to fitness clearance. But it's the T20I series — and specifically, Sooryavanshi's potential debut — that has captured the imagination.

## The Bigger Picture

At 15 years and five months, Sooryavanshi isn't just a cricket prodigy. He's become a cultural event. His parents travelling with the team. A separate dressing room. Safeguarding risk assessments at five English counties. A former England captain publicly strategising about how to tire him out.

BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia confirmed the board is covering the travel and accommodation expenses for Sooryavanshi's parents, an arrangement made specifically because of his age. It's the kind of logistical detail that underscores just how unusual this situation is.

The last time cricket saw anything comparable was Sachin Tendulkar's debut at 16 against Pakistan in 1989. Tendulkar didn't need safeguarding protocols — the world was a different place. But like Tendulkar, Sooryavanshi arrives with the kind of anticipation that can either launch a career or crush a teenager under its weight.

Durham, Wednesday, July 1. England versus India. Sooryavanshi, if selected, will walk out to bat having potentially fielded for 20 overs, using a dressing room separate from his teammates, with Michael Vaughan's prediction ringing in every commentator's ear.

He's 15. He holds the IPL sixes record. And the whole cricketing world is watching.
